content: Over the past few months I have spoken to several people about lean and have consistently gotten the question "Can you also write papers about that?". The implicit question being whether there is any academic recognition to be gained by formalizing content into lean, in particular outside the lean community. I have seen some papers about mathlib in general, and autoformalization gets plenty of papers. However, I am unaware of whether it is possible to submit papers to journals for this or other possibilities, when you simply formalize an active area of research or the needed preliminaries. Can you help me with this questions I am getting?

I'm happy to share my personal opinion. It is informed by being a mathlib maintainer, but inherently subjective. In short:

  • some papers "we have formalized X" are mere proof of work papers: they demonstrate that you have done it, but no further insights. Whether these were publishable back then may already have been contentious. These days, it definitely won't suffice. So, a mere "I formalized X" won't cut it.
  • As a corollary: if you auto-formalize X and that's it, that by itself is imho not worth a paper. (Especially these days, where almost any X can be auto-formalized if you're patient enough, or perhaps clever enough in using a good harness.)
  • One goal of formalization should be to improve understanding: of the mathematics involved, of the best way to formalize (e.g. design decisions, how to make things ergonomic, tooling to make this easier, etc.) Any insights gained there are imho very much worth publishing!

In other words: focus on understanding what is happening, what you can learn about formalization, what others formalizing (a related or a different area) can take away from your work. Then it can be interesting!
This space is moving fast, so predicting the future is hard. But I believe that the above still has one.

In general: formalization used to be an extremely niche topic --- so you could get papers there, but whether a regular math department would find them interesting, hire you as a PhD student/postdoc/faculty based on that was unclear. It's getting more mainstream now... but math departments tend to be conservative.

So, switching your career to formalization is a somewhat risky move from the point of optimising your academic prospect. On the other hand, I've personally become much happier through that switch (so would do it again). But you should make this choice consciously.

A historical comment: in the 2010s when I was pushing the formalization of basic undergraduate mathematics, this was a common question I got from researchers: "how can I get a paper from formalizing a bunch of undergraduate material which everyone knows is correct?". If the Lean community had focussed on publications rather than making a wonderful library then we would not be where we are today. But I appreciate that for an academic this is an important question. A bunch of the early contributors to mathlib were undergraduates, who were not asking that kind of question at that time.

Note that when I'm hiring I definitely look at non-standard academic sources of "credit", such as contributions to open source libraries like Mathlib.
This is very far from the norm in mathematics, but last week at a Math & AI workshop I argued that mathematicians should more broadly consider this. That said, it will takes ages to change such norms in mathematics.

Allow me to mention the Annals of Formalized Mathematics, which tries to address the problems here from a few directions: it's a math journal that publishes formalization papers that might not fit in any other math journal, while also trying to raise the prestige of this kind of work. There's a lot of formalization work that isn't suited for a paper at all, and I would love to see more recognition for this -- but the AFM is an option to consider.
